prompt: Why does a model asked to continue a question-and-answer text often write another question after its answer?
hint: What usually follows an answer in such a text?

choices.text: The next question is the likeliest continuation
choices.why: Right. Nothing in the model treats one answer as the end of the job.

choices.text: It misunderstood the prompt and thought you asked two questions
choices.why: No misunderstanding is needed. It continues text, and in that text a question follows an answer.

choices.text: Its output limit was set too high
choices.why: A lower limit cuts at a count, not after the answer. The cause is what is likely next.

choices.text: Temperature 0 forces it to keep writing
choices.why: At temperature 0 `toylm` stopped after `yes.` The run-on came from a draw at temperature 1.

hint: Three reasons a loop can end.

choices.text: The model chose to stop
choices.why: That is `end`.

choices.text: The token limit was reached
choices.why: That is `length`.

choices.text: The user interrupted the run
choices.why: Nobody interrupted anything. The loop checked the text and found the stop.

choices.text: A stop sequence appeared in the output, and the text was cut before it
choices.why: Right. The third reason beside `end` and `length`.

prompt: With `--stop question`, seed 1 printed `yes.` and not `yes. question`. Where did the word `question` go?
hint: Is the stop text part of the answer?

choices.text: The model was told not to write it
choices.why: The model never sees the stop sequence. The loop does the work.

choices.text: It was never generated
choices.why: It was: the output count was 3 tokens for 2 shown, and the third was `question`.

choices.text: It was written, then removed with the stop
choices.why: Right. The loop found it in the text and cut the output just before it.

choices.text: It moved to the end of the prompt
choices.why: The prompt is not changed by generation.

prompt: `toylm generate ... --stop question` printed `yes.` with `output 3 tokens`. How many of those tokens are visible in the output?
Of eight seeds, how many outputs did adding `--stop question` change?
hint: Compare the two lists of eight.

choices.text: All eight, since the stop applies to every run
choices.why: It is checked in every run, and it fires only where the text appears.

choices.text: One, seed 1, which had run on
choices.why: Right. A stop changes only runs that reach it; the other seven never wrote `question`.

choices.text: None of them
choices.why: Seed 1 lost its invented second question.

choices.text: Four, the ones that answered `yes`
choices.why: The `yes` answers that ended on their own were unchanged.

prompt: None of the eight answers to `when does the café open ?` said `seven`, though the corpus answers it with `at seven` twice. Why?
hint: What did the first capture say the model looked at?

choices.text: `toylm` sees only `answer :`, not the question
choices.why: Right. The question is outside its two-word window, so it answers with the commonest continuation of `answer :`.

choices.text: The stop sequence removed `seven` from every answer
choices.why: Without the stop the answers were the same. The stop only removed a second question.

choices.text: `seven` has no count after `answer :` because of the stop
choices.why: Counts come from the corpus. `at` does follow `answer :`, and then `six` or `seven`.

choices.text: Temperature 1 prevents the likeliest word from ever winning
choices.why: At temperature 1 the likeliest word wins most draws. `yes` was the likeliest after `answer :`.

prompt: What does a stop sequence do for the correctness of an answer?
hint: Read the last paragraph of the section.

choices.text: It guarantees the answer is the first one the model meant
choices.why: It only cuts text. The first answer can be wrong, as `yes` was.

choices.text: It forces the model to answer the question asked
choices.why: The model never sees the stop sequence.

choices.text: It removes invented facts from the reply
choices.why: It removes text after a marker, invented or not.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. It decides where the answer ends; whether the answer is right is another problem.

prompt: `--stop and` turned `soup, bread and cake.` into `soup, bread`. What went wrong?

choices.text: `and` is too long for a stop
choices.why: Length is not the problem; a short common string is the problem.

choices.text: The stop only works at temperature 1
choices.why: It worked, at temperature 0. It just worked in the wrong place.

choices.text: The stop text occurs inside a legitimate answer
choices.why: Right. A stop fires wherever its text appears, including inside an answer you wanted whole.

choices.text: The limit cut the answer
choices.why: The finish reason was `stop`, not `length`.

prompt: `--stop at` turned `cold and the cat wakes.` into `cold and the c`. Why?

choices.text: `at` is a reserved word in `toylm`
choices.why: No word is reserved. It is a plain text comparison.

choices.text: The stop matched the `at` in the prompt
choices.why: Only the generated text is checked, not the prompt.

choices.text: It matches text, and `cat` contains `at`
choices.why: Right. A stop is a substring test, so a short stop fires inside longer words.

choices.text: The model chose to end mid-word
choices.why: The model chose `cat`. The loop cut it.

prompt: Why is a stop that fires inside an answer harder to notice than a limit that cuts one?

choices.text: A stop removes the whole answer
choices.why: It removes only what follows the stop text.

choices.text: Ending on `stop` looks like success
choices.why: Right. `length` says something was cut; `stop` is what a working stop also reports.

choices.text: Stops are applied after the reply reaches your program
choices.why: The loop applies them while generating.

choices.text: Limits always produce an error message from the API that is shown to the user
choices.why: A limit produces `length`, not an error. Your code has to check it.

prompt: Your program needs the marker that triggered the stop. What should it do?
hint: Is the stop text in the output?

choices.text: Add the marker back itself
choices.why: Right. The stop text is not included in the output, in `toylm` or in most model APIs.

choices.text: Read it from the output, where it is the last word
choices.why: It is not there; the output ends just before it.

choices.text: Choose a longer stop so that it is kept
choices.why: Length does not decide whether it is kept.

choices.text: Ask the model in the prompt to repeat the stop text twice
choices.why: Then the first one fires and the second is never written.

prompt: You prompt with `question :` and want only the question. Which stop fits?
hint: Which label starts the other side's turn?

choices.text: `question`
choices.why: That label is already in the prompt; the turn you want follows it.
A question mark can end the turn, and it can also appear inside a longer question.

choices.text: No stop: the model writes one turn and then waits
choices.why: Without a stop `toylm` wrote the answer as well.

choices.text: `answer`
choices.why: Right. It begins the next turn, so stopping there keeps exactly the question.

prompt: Which of these make a good stop sequence? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It marks the end of the unit you want
choices.why: Yes. That is what a stop is for.

choices.text: It cannot occur inside a legitimate answer
choices.why: Yes. Otherwise it cuts answers you wanted whole.

choices.text: It has been seen to fire on real replies
choices.why: Yes. A stop you never saw fire has not been tested.

choices.text: It is as short as possible
choices.why: Short strings occur by accident, like `at` inside `cat`.

prompt: When `--stop` is given twice, generation ends at whichever of the two appears ___.
Match each run to its finish reason.
A chat assistant built on plain text with `User:` and `Assistant:` labels sometimes writes a `User:` line of its own. What is the risk, and the fix?
hint: Who would that line be attributed to?

choices.text: An invented user turn could be acted on; stop at `User:`
choices.why: Right. The model is putting words in the user's mouth. Stopping at the next turn's label keeps only the assistant's turn.

choices.text: The reply gets longer; lower the token limit
choices.why: A limit cuts at a count and may let a short invented turn through.

choices.text: Nothing; the program ignores labels
choices.why: The program may well read that line as input from the user.

choices.text: The model is confused; raise the temperature
choices.why: A higher temperature makes run-ons more likely, not less.
